section.title: The Conclusion of the Matter
section.sectionRationale: The book ends with an epilogue that steps back to commend the Teacher and his work, and then delivers the verdict the whole book has been driving toward. After all the honest wrestling with a fleeting world, the words of the wise are given as goads and nails, and the conclusion of the matter is stated plainly: fear God and keep His commandments, for God will bring every deed into judgment. This is where the whole book lands.
section.thesis: The Teacher's hard, honest words are a gift from the one Shepherd, and their whole point resolves here: fear God and keep His commandments, for God will judge every deed, so a fleeting life finds its meaning in reverent obedience to the God who made and will assess it.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the epilogue commending the Teacher, whose wise words are like goads and firmly embedded nails given by one Shepherd; and the conclusion of the whole matter, fear God, keep His commandments, and reckon with the coming judgment.

units.label: The Teacher's words are goads and nails

verses.text: Not only was the {{qoheleth|Teacher}} wise, but he also taught the people knowledge; he pondered, searched out, and arranged many proverbs.
The Teacher searched to find delightful sayings and to record accurate words of truth.
The words of the wise are like goads, and the anthologies of the masters are like firmly embedded nails driven by a single Shepherd.
And by these, my son, be further warned: There is no end to the making of many books, and much study wearies the body.

units.label: The conclusion of the matter
units.note: fear God and keep His commandments

verses.text: When all has been heard, the conclusion of the matter is this: {{yare|Fear}} God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man.
For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil.

qoheleth.gloss: The Teacher or Preacher, the title that names the book's speaker and gives Ecclesiastes its name. It comes from the word for an assembly or congregation, so the Qoheleth is the one who gathers a people to teach them. The epilogue steps back to commend this teacher and to hand his hard, honest words to us as a gift.

yare.gloss: To fear, revere, stand in awe. To fear God is not mere fright but reverent trust and obedience before the Maker and Judge of all. It is the beginning of wisdom in the wider wisdom tradition, and here it is the conclusion of the whole matter, the settled response to a fleeting world and a coming judgment.

basic.context: The book closes with a short epilogue that pulls back the camera. Someone commends the Teacher: he was wise, he taught the people, he searched and arranged his sayings carefully, and he wrote honest, accurate words of truth. Those words, we are told, are like cattle goads that prod us forward and like firmly driven nails that hold, and they come ultimately from one Shepherd, that is, from God. Then comes the verdict the whole book has been building toward. When everything has been heard, here is the bottom line: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole duty of every person, because God will bring every single deed, even the hidden ones, good or evil, into judgment.
basic.hermeneutics: People debate how to read this ending. Some hear the fear God and keep His commandments as a later, more orthodox editor tidying up a dangerous book. But it reads far better as the intended climax: the whole book has stripped away every idol under the sun so that only the fear of God is left standing. The word hevel, fleeting, has run through the book not to make us despair but to drive us to the one thing that is not vapor, reverent trust and obedience toward God, who sees and will judge all.
basic.originalLanguages: The speaker is the Qoheleth, the Teacher or Preacher, the one who gathers a congregation to instruct them. His words come from one Shepherd, a picture of God as the true source of wisdom. And the conclusion turns on yare, to fear: to fear God is not cringing dread but reverent awe, trust, and obedience before the Maker and Judge of all.
basic.typology: The one Shepherd who drives home the words of the wise points to Christ, the good Shepherd and the wisdom of God in person, in whom all the goads and nails of Scripture find their center. The coming judgment of every deed points to the day when God will judge the world through the risen Christ, who is both the Judge and the Savior who bore that judgment for His people.
basic.christ: The fear of God that the book calls for finds its fullness in Christ, who feared God perfectly and taught us to reverence the Father. The judgment of every deed, even hidden things, is the judgment seat of Christ, before whom all must appear. Yet the good news is that the Judge is also the one who was made subject to futility for us and bore our judgment at the cross, so that those who fear God in Him need not fear that day.
basic.god: God stands over the whole book as Creator, Shepherd, and Judge. He is the source of true wisdom, the one whose commandments give shape to a fleeting life, and the one who will bring everything into account, including what is hidden. To fear Him is to know that nothing is lost or overlooked, and that reverent obedience is never in vain.
basic.crossReferences: Proverbs 1 says the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. John 10 names Jesus the good Shepherd. Second Corinthians 5 says all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ. First Corinthians 15 says in the Lord our labor is not in vain.
basic.oneStory: Ecclesiastes has cleared the ground of every false hope under the sun, and here it plants the one thing that stands: fear God, keep His commandments, and live before the coming judgment. That resolution reaches its fullness in Christ, the true Shepherd and the Judge who bore our judgment, in whom a fleeting life is finally given weight and meaning.

context.literary:
Ecclesiastes has a frame. The book opens with a title and a motto, Ecclesiastes 1:1-2, and these verses close it. Between them nearly everything is spoken by the Teacher in the first person, 'I saw,' 'I said in my heart.' Here the voice changes. The Teacher is spoken about in the third person, and the one speaking addresses 'my son,' verse 12. Most readers hear a second voice, a father or a teacher of wisdom who hands the book on to the next generation and tells the son how to read it.

The epilogue has three small movements. Verses 9 and 10 commend the Teacher's craft: he taught, weighed, searched and arranged, and he wrote honestly. Verse 11 says what such words are for and where they come from. Verses 12 to 14 give the warning and the verdict. The scene moves from the author, to the words, to the reader, to God. The final sentence is built simply: two imperatives, fear and keep, followed by a single reason introduced with 'for.'

The epilogue also answers the opening. The Teacher began with 'Everything is futile,' and the epilogue does not deny it. It places it. Futility is the honest report from under the sun, and the last word comes from above it. Notice too that verse 14 returns to a note struck much earlier, that 'God will judge the righteous and the wicked,' Ecclesiastes 3:17. The book ends on a theme it has been circling all along, and the closing verse of the whole book is a verse about judgment, not about mood.
context.historical:
Wisdom writing in the ancient Near East was a schoolroom and court tradition. Scribes collected sayings, arranged them in anthologies and passed them to young men being trained for service. Verse 9 uses the language of that craft. The Teacher 'arranged many proverbs,' and verse 11 speaks of 'anthologies,' which fits the world of Israel's wisdom teachers, who set sayings in order for memory and use. Solomon is credited elsewhere with three thousand proverbs, 1 Kings 4:32, and the book presents its Teacher as 'the son of David, king in Jerusalem,' Ecclesiastes 1:1.

The two images of verse 11 come from the farm. A goad was a pointed stick used to steer an ox in the furrow. It stung, but it kept the animal on the line. Paul hears the same picture in the words of the risen Christ, 'It is hard for you to kick against the goads,' Acts 26:14. Nails, or tent pegs, fixed a thing in place so that it would hold in wind. The words of the wise therefore do two jobs. They move the sluggish and they secure the wandering.

The warning about many books in verse 12 would have landed in a culture that prized writing and copying. Egypt and Mesopotamia produced libraries of instruction literature, and a young scribe could be tempted to think that more reading was always more wisdom. The epilogue tells him that study has no natural end and no natural rest, and that learning cannot supply by volume the one thing it needs, a right relation to God.

The 'single Shepherd' was a familiar picture for a king and for God. Israel's own psalms say 'The LORD is my shepherd,' Psalm 23:1, and the prophets promise that God will appoint one shepherd over His people, Ezekiel 34:23.
context.canonical:
The verdict of verse 13 gathers a line of teaching that runs through Israel's Scriptures. Moses asked what the LORD requires, 'to fear the LORD your God by walking in all His ways, to love Him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD,' Deuteronomy 10:12-13. The wisdom books open the same way, 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge,' Proverbs 1:7, and 'the beginning of wisdom,' Proverbs 9:10. Ecclesiastes itself has prepared for the verdict: 'Therefore, fear God,' Ecclesiastes 5:7, and 'it will go well with those who fear God,' Ecclesiastes 8:12.

The judgment of verse 14 is picked up in the New Testament with a new name attached. God judges 'men's secrets through Christ Jesus,' Romans 2:16. 'We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad,' 2 Corinthians 5:10. Paul says that the Lord 'will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men's hearts,' 1 Corinthians 4:5, and Jesus says that people will give an account 'for every careless word,' Matthew 12:36. The epilogue's claim that nothing is hidden is repeated in Hebrews 4:13.

The single Shepherd becomes Jesus, 'I am the good shepherd,' John 10:11, and Hebrews calls Him 'that great Shepherd of the sheep,' Hebrews 13:20.

The canon also made room for the book. Jewish tradition debated whether Ecclesiastes belonged among the sacred writings, and these closing verses, with their clear fear of God and commandment keeping, were part of what settled the matter in its favor.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The epilogue is the author's instruction on how to read everything that came before. He wants the young reader to take the Teacher seriously and not to be scandalized. The hard sayings about death, injustice and wasted labor are not a loss of faith. They are 'accurate words of truth,' verse 10, spoken by a wise man who looked straight at a fallen world and did not look away.

He also wants the reader to receive the book as given by God and not merely as one man's opinion. The goads and nails are driven 'by a single Shepherd,' verse 11. The reader is not asked to sort the Teacher's words into acceptable and unacceptable. He is asked to be moved and steadied by all of them.

Then comes the demand. The author does not close with a theory of life. He closes with two verbs, fear and keep, and a reason, a coming judgment of everything including what is hidden. The first hearers were meant to leave the book changed in how they live, not better informed. The warning against endless books is part of the same aim: the wise man would rather have his son obey God than own a library.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of Ecclesiastes describes how life looks under the sun, and the Teacher's reports of what he saw and felt are not commands. This closing passage is different. Verses 13 and 14 are prescriptive: fear God, keep His commandments, and live as someone who will give account. The imperatives are the point of the book, and the earlier descriptions are what make them credible.

That shapes how to apply the rest. It would be a mistake to treat a line like 'Eat your food with joy,' or a bleak report about death, as a rule of life apart from the epilogue. Equally, it would be a mistake to treat verse 13 as a grim duty with no joy in it. The book has already told the reader to enjoy God's gifts, Ecclesiastes 11:9 among them, and that verse also ends with judgment. The commands of verse 13 do not cancel delight. They give it a frame.

The warning in verse 12 is addressed to a particular son, but its principle stands: study that never turns into obedience wearies the body and leaves the heart where it was. It is not a ban on reading.

debates.question: Who is speaking in the epilogue, and does it fit the rest of the book?

views.label: The Teacher himself, speaking about himself
views.case: Some read verses 9 to 14 as the Teacher stepping back and describing his own work in the third person, as he sometimes does with the title 'Teacher' elsewhere in the book. On this reading the whole book is one voice and the verdict is his.

views.label: A second wise voice who frames the Teacher
views.case: Many scholars note that the Teacher is spoken about here, that 'my son' appears, and that the opening of the book, Ecclesiastes 1:1, is also in the third person. They see a frame narrator who presents and endorses the Teacher's words to a student. This fits the language of 'one Shepherd,' which is a statement about where the words come from.

views.label: A later editor who corrects a gloomy book
views.case: A few argue that verses 13 and 14 were added to tame the book's skepticism with orthodoxy. The case rests on a tone change, and it assumes that fear of God and doubt about life under the sun cannot belong together.

debates.bearing: The third reading has the least support, because the call to fear God is not new here. The Teacher has already said 'Therefore, fear God,' Ecclesiastes 5:7, and 'it will go well with those who fear God,' Ecclesiastes 8:12. Whether one voice or two is behind the epilogue, the church has received it as the book's own conclusion, and the epilogue itself says that the words are given by a single Shepherd.

debates.question: What does 'this is the whole duty of man' mean?

views.label: The whole of what a person must do
views.case: This is the sense the BSB gives. The Hebrew has just a short phrase that can be read as 'this is all of man,' and translators supply 'duty.' On this view the verse names the sum of a person's obligation.

views.label: The whole of what a person is
views.case: Others keep the phrase closer to the Hebrew: fear and obedience are the whole of man, what a human being is made for. Humanity finds its meaning in being a creature that reverences its Creator.

views.label: The whole of what a person is to keep in view
views.case: A third reading takes the phrase as 'this is everything for every person,' stressing that nothing else in the book's long search outranks it.

debates.bearing: The readings agree in practice. Fear and obedience are not an addition to a life, they are the shape of a life lived rightly. The second reading is attractive because it fits the Teacher's own story: a man who tried everything under the sun learned what he was for.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 9 lists three verbs for the Teacher's work: he 'pondered, searched out, and arranged.' The first, izzen, is the verb the BSB renders 'pondered,' a careful weighing of a saying before it is passed on. The second, chiqqer, means to search and probe, and it is the verb of careful investigation. The third, tiqqen, means to set straight, to put in order. The three together describe a scribe who weighs a saying, tests it and arranges it, a picture of wisdom as hard craft, not casual opinion. Verse 10 adds that he sought 'delightful sayings,' words of delight, chefetz, and 'accurate words of truth.' The BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew can be read 'and sought to write what was upright and true.' Either way, the Teacher was after words that are both pleasing and true, and the epilogue says he did not trade one for the other.

Verse 11 gives the images. The 'goads' are dorbanot, the pointed sticks that drive oxen, and the 'nails' are masmerot, fixed pegs or spikes. The anthologies are the 'masters of collections,' a Hebrew phrase for those who gather and arrange sayings. The BSB's 'masters of anthologies' keeps that sense. Then comes ro'eh echad, 'one Shepherd.' The BSB footnote notes the word can also be read simply as 'shepherd.' Whether one reads 'one' as a number or as a title, the claim is the same: these words have a single, divine source, even though many hands collected them.

The word 'fear' in verse 13 is the verb yare, from the same root as the noun yir'ah, the fear of the LORD. The verb has a range. It can mean to be afraid, as when people fear danger, and it can mean reverence. The phrase is not a command to feel dread of a monster. It is the fear of one who knows who is standing before him. Ecclesiastes uses the verb with God as its object at 3:14, 5:7, 7:18 and 8:12 to 13, so the epilogue gathers a thread. The phrase 'keep His commandments' uses shamar, the verb of guarding, which Genesis uses of the man's task to 'keep' the garden, Genesis 2:15. Obedience is guarding something precious, not merely complying.

The phrase 'the conclusion of the matter' translates sof davar, literally 'the end of the word' or 'the end of the matter.' Davar is the ordinary word for both a word and a thing, so the phrase can mean the last word and the bottom line at once. The BSB's 'when all has been heard' keeps the sense that the whole book must be listened to before its verdict is given.

Finally, verse 14 pairs 'every deed,' kol ma'aseh, with 'every hidden thing,' kol ne'elam. The second is the participle of a verb meaning to hide. Judgment reaches what was concealed, whether 'good or evil.' The word mishpat, judgment, is the same word the Teacher used at 3:16 for the place of justice, where he saw wickedness.

typology.type: The one Shepherd who drives the words home, verse 11
typology.fulfillment: Israel's picture of God as shepherd, Psalm 23:1, narrows in the prophets to a single shepherd-king from David's line, Ezekiel 34:23. Jesus claims the title, 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11, and Hebrews calls Him 'that great Shepherd of the sheep,' Hebrews 13:20. The correspondence is that the words of the wise come from one source who leads. The escalation is that the Shepherd is also the Word, who becomes the Lamb. The type falls short in that Ecclesiastes names the Shepherd but does not show Him bearing the wounds of His flock.

The goad drives and the nail secures. The risen Christ uses the goad for Saul, Acts 26:14, a prod that turned a persecutor around. Paul, in turn, calls Christ's people to be 'steadfast and immovable,' 1 Corinthians 15:58, language close to the nail's work. The Scripture does the stinging and the fixing, and in the New Testament the Shepherd Himself is the one at work in it, Hebrews 4:12. This is a picture rather than a prophecy. It shows what Scripture does, and the New Testament shows who is doing it.

typology.type: The Judge of every deed and the hidden things
typology.fulfillment: The epilogue ends with a judge who sees all. The New Testament names the Judge's agent, 'God will judge men's secrets through Christ Jesus,' Romans 2:16, and says all must appear before His seat, 2 Corinthians 5:10. The escalation is a double one. The Judge is also the one who 'laid down His life,' John 10:11, so the very person who sees every hidden deed is the one who bore the penalty for the deeds of His people. The type is incomplete without that turn, because the epilogue by itself offers no account of how a person who has failed to keep the commandments can stand.

study.christ:
The epilogue leads to Christ by three routes, and none of them needs an allegory. The first is contrast. Ecclesiastes is the book of the wise man who ran out of road. The Teacher had wisdom, wealth and time, and he had to say that everything was futile. The epilogue answers by pointing outside himself to a Shepherd. In the New Testament Paul says that in Christ 'are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,' Colossians 2:3. Where the Teacher searched and arranged, Christ is wisdom given as a person. Where the Teacher could only say that every deed will be judged, Christ is the one through whom that judgment comes, Romans 2:16.

The second route is the fear of God. The call to fear God and keep His commandments is exactly the call that Israel failed. Deuteronomy asked for fear, love, service and obedience with all the heart and soul, Deuteronomy 10:12-13, and the prophets recorded that the people did not do it. Jesus is the one person who did. He kept the commandments perfectly, and He feared the Father in the full sense of the word, with love, trust and obedience even to death. So the verdict of verse 13 is both a summons to us and a description of Him. Believers are not saved by now keeping what Jesus kept. They are united to the one who kept it, and then they are enabled to follow Him, 1 Corinthians 15:58.

The third route is judgment. Verse 14 is a sobering sentence, and the Teacher does not say how anyone could survive it. The New Testament does. The Judge who will bring every hidden thing to light, 1 Corinthians 4:5, is the same one who 'lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11. The cross is where the judgment of verse 14 was taken on behalf of those who trust Him. It does not make the verse harmless. It makes the verse bearable, because the person who sees everything is the person who has already loved us at our worst.

One caution. The text does not mention the Messiah, and it is better to say that Christ fulfills its hope than to claim that the Teacher saw Him. The epilogue is a signpost, and the New Testament walks the road.
study.god:
The epilogue gives a short but full portrait of God. He is first the giver of wisdom. The words of the wise come from 'a single Shepherd,' which means that truth about life is not something people extract by effort alone. It is something God provides, gently and firmly, with goads and nails. A shepherd does not shout at sheep from a distance. He is near enough to use a stick on the ones that stray and a hand on the ones that tire.

He is also the God who commands. The book that began by listing what cannot be gained under the sun ends with a God who has spoken clearly about what to do. 'Keep His commandments' assumes that He has made His will known. The doctrine of God that rules here is not a remote first cause but a Lord who speaks, whose words can be kept, and whose words are good for those who keep them, as Deuteronomy 10:13 says, 'for your own good.'

He is the judge of everything. Nothing in creation is hidden from Him, Hebrews 4:13, and that includes motives, secrets and deeds that no human court will ever try. The Teacher saw injustice and could not make sense of it, Ecclesiastes 3:16-17, and here is the answer: God has not overlooked it. A tension is held together in the verse. God judges, and 'it will go well with those who fear God,' Ecclesiastes 8:12. His judgment is not arbitrary, and it is a comfort to the wronged as much as a warning to the wrongdoer.

A further tension is that the same God has set the Teacher to a 'heavy burden,' Ecclesiastes 1:13, and also gives wisdom and joy to the one who pleases Him, Ecclesiastes 2:26. The epilogue does not resolve that tension by explaining it. It resolves it by directing the reader to fear Him.

For worship, the passage teaches that the right posture before God is reverence that issues in obedience, not mere enthusiasm. A person who has learned that everything will be weighed will pray differently, work differently, speak differently and hide less. The fear of God is not the opposite of joy. In this book it is what makes joy safe.

crossReferences.note: The motto of the book, 'Futility of futilities... Everything is futile.' The epilogue returns to it without taking it back. The futility is real for life apart from God, and the closing verses show where the weight lies, in fear and obedience before the God who judges.

The Teacher says in his heart that God will judge the righteous and the wicked, since there is a time for every deed. This is the earlier form of the epilogue's last verse. The book ends on a claim it had been making quietly from the middle.

After a warning about many dreams and many words, the Teacher says, 'Therefore, fear God.' This is the earlier use of the same verb as in 12:13. The fear of God is the Teacher's repeated answer to the emptiness he describes, not a late addition.

'He who fears God will follow both warnings.' The Teacher has been warning against both too much righteousness and too much wickedness, and he says that the person who fears God will hold both warnings. The fear of God keeps a person balanced where wisdom alone cannot.

A command to rejoice in youth, followed by 'know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment.' The ending of the chapter before the epilogue joins joy and judgment, which shows that the judgment of 12:14 does not abolish enjoyment but gives it meaning.

The strongest background to 12:13. Moses asks what the LORD requires, and the answer joins fear, love, service and keeping the commandments. The Teacher's verdict is a wisdom form of the law's central demand, spoken to a new generation.

'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.' Proverbs treats the fear of God as the starting point of wisdom, and Ecclesiastes treats it as the end of the road. Between them they say that wisdom begins and finishes in the same place.

The prophet states the requirement in other words: act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God. It confirms that the law, the prophets and the wise all point to one life of reverent obedience, which is why the Teacher can call it the whole of man.

Christ's word to Saul on the Damascus road: 'It is hard for you to kick against the goads.' The goad of 12:11 appears here in the mouth of the risen Lord. He is the Shepherd who prods a wandering sheep and turns a persecutor around.

Paul says that God will judge men's secrets through Christ Jesus. This answers 'every hidden thing' in 12:14 and names the agent of judgment. The Teacher's verse about judgment is read in the New Testament as a verse about the day Christ comes.

'We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.' The believer is included here, and the language of 'things done in the body, whether good or bad' echoes 'good or evil' in 12:14. Paul adds that the fear of the Lord moves him to persuade others, 5:11.

After the long argument about resurrection, Paul says that labor in the Lord is not in vain. This answers the Teacher's repeated complaint about toil, Ecclesiastes 2:11, with a resurrection that makes work in the Lord count.

study.oneStory:
Ecclesiastes answers a question that the early chapters of Genesis raise. God made the world good, and the human task in it was to work and keep the garden, Genesis 2:15. After the fall the ground is cursed and a person's labor is 'through toil,' Genesis 3:17. The Teacher is the Bible's wise man who stands inside that curse and tells the truth about it. Futility, hevel, is the same word as the name of Abel, whose short life is the first picture of how fragile human days are, Genesis 4. The book tells the story of the fallen world from the inside.

The epilogue then points forward. A fallen world needs a Shepherd who speaks, a Judge who sees and, as the rest of Scripture reveals, a Savior who bears. The fear of God is the posture of the people of God in every age, from Abraham, of whom the angel says 'now I know that you fear God,' Genesis 22:12, to the redeemed who sing of the Lord's works in Revelation 15:3-4. The New Testament takes verse 14 and attaches a name to it. Jesus will judge, and the one who will judge is the one who died, Romans 2:16, John 10:11.

The story ends where the Teacher could only hope. In the new creation, the labor that was futility becomes work that is not in vain, 1 Corinthians 15:58. The hidden things are brought to light and, for those who are in Christ, there is nothing left to fear in the exposure. The goads and nails of Scripture do their work until the Shepherd gathers the flock, and the long search under the sun ends in the presence of the One who was the answer from the start.

For the reader, this means that Ecclesiastes is not a detour in the Bible's story. It is the honest middle of it, written for a people who live after Genesis 3 and before Revelation, who need to hear that their days are fleeting and that God is not. It prepares a person to hear the gospel by taking away every other hope and then telling the truth about the one hope that stays.

quiz.q: How does the epilogue describe the words of the wise?

options.text: Like goads and firmly embedded nails, given by one Shepherd.
options.note: The images picture words that prod us forward and hold fast, sourced in God Himself.

options.text: As sharp, lasting words that come ultimately from God.
options.note: A fair summary, though the specific images of goads, nails, and the one Shepherd carry the point.

options.text: As gentle sayings meant only to comfort.
options.note: Goads prod and nails fix; these words unsettle and hold, not merely soothe.

options.text: As merely human opinions with no authority.
options.note: They come from one Shepherd, God, and carry His authority.

quiz.q: What is the conclusion of the matter when all has been heard?

options.text: Fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.
options.note: This is the plain verdict the whole book has been driving toward.

options.text: Revere God and live in obedience to Him.
options.note: Faithful in substance, though the exact call to fear God and keep His commandments is the point.

options.text: Enjoy life and stop asking hard questions.
options.note: The book commends joy, but its conclusion is the fear of God, not the end of questions.

options.text: There is no conclusion; everything is meaningless.
options.note: The book gives a clear conclusion, the fear of God under the coming judgment.

quiz.q: Why does the fear of God matter so urgently, according to the final verse?

options.text: Because God will bring every deed, even hidden ones, into judgment, whether good or evil.
options.note: The certainty of a comprehensive judgment grounds the call to fear God.

options.text: Because God pays attention to what people do.
options.note: True, but understates the point: a full judgment of every deed, including the hidden.

options.text: Because fearing God guarantees an easy and prosperous life.
options.note: The motive given is the coming judgment, not a promise of ease.

options.text: Because God ignores what is done in secret.
options.note: The verse says the opposite: even every hidden thing comes into judgment.

quiz.q: What does the refrain hevel, fleeting or futile, do across the book?

options.text: It exposes the limits of everything under the sun so we anchor in the God who is not fleeting.
options.note: Hevel drives the reader away from idols and toward the fear of God.

options.text: It shows that life under the sun cannot be mastered or held onto.
options.note: True about brevity and elusiveness, though its purpose is to push us to God.

options.text: It proves that life is worthless and not worth living.
options.note: Hevel means breath-brief, not worthless; the book still commends enjoying God's gifts.

options.text: It teaches that God's own work is pointless.
options.note: The futility is of life under the sun apart from God, not of God's work.

quiz.q: How should we read fear God and keep His commandments in 12:13-14?

options.text: As the intended climax that resolves the book, gathering all its wrestling into the one thing that stands.
options.note: The book empties every hope under the sun so the fear of God can remain as its resolution.

options.text: As the book's clear and orthodox conclusion about how to live.
options.note: True, and best understood as the deliberate climax the whole argument has sought.

options.text: As a stray comment loosely attached to the end.
options.note: The fear of God has surfaced throughout the book; the ending gathers rather than intrudes.

options.text: As a denial of everything the book has said.
options.note: It resolves the book's tension rather than contradicting it.

quiz.q: How does the coming judgment connect to Christ?

options.text: It is the judgment seat of Christ, who is both the Judge and the one who bore our judgment for those who fear God in Him.
options.note: God will judge the world through the risen Christ, who also saves His people from that judgment.

options.text: It points to a final day when God will judge every person.
options.note: True, and the New Testament names Christ as the one through whom God will judge.

options.text: It has no link to Christ at all.
options.note: Scripture ties the judgment of every deed directly to Christ, 2 Corinthians 5:10 and Acts 17:31.

options.text: It means believers will still be condemned for their sins.
options.note: Christ bore the judgment so that those who are His are received, not condemned.

questions: The Teacher's words are called goads that prod us forward. Where has the honesty of Ecclesiastes unsettled you and pushed you toward God rather than away from Him?
The whole book lands on fear God and keep His commandments. What would it look like for reverent trust and obedience to become the center of your life rather than one part of it?
God will bring every deed, even the hidden, into judgment. How does living before a God who sees everything change the way you handle what no one else knows?
Ecclesiastes strips away every hope under the sun to leave only the fear of God. What lesser hopes is it inviting you to loosen your grip on right now?
The Judge of every deed is also the one who bore our judgment at the cross. How does knowing Christ as both Judge and Savior free you to face that coming day without terror?

translationNotes.note: Teacher translates Qoheleth, from the word for an assembly, so the title means the one who gathers and addresses a congregation; it is the name that gives the book its Hebrew title.
A single Shepherd may be capitalized as a reference to God, the ultimate source of the words of the wise; some editions render it shepherd, but the sense of God as the giver of true wisdom stands.
Fear translates yare, reverent awe, trust, and obedience before God, not mere fright; to fear God is the settled response the whole book has sought.
The whole duty of man renders a phrase that is literally this is the whole of man; the fear of God and obedience are what a human life, in the end, is all about.
